name: Pattern 3: Adaptive Practice
title: Pattern 3: Adaptive Practice
answer: Adaptive practice is software that watches how a student answers and changes the next question, giving harder items after a run of correct answers and easier ones after a run of mistakes. It matters because it is one of the oldest forms of AI in schools and can help teachers regroup students, but its practice scores can rise while real understanding stays flat. The teacher still decides how to use what the software learned and how to check learning without the tool.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: Adaptive practice is one of the oldest forms of AI in schools. The software watches a student's answers and adjusts the next question, so a string of right answers leads to harder items and a string of mistakes leads to easier ones. Programs such as Zearn for elementary math and Khan Academy for older grades work in this way. The teacher's role is to read what the software learned and use that information to regroup students the next day. The problem it addresses is matching practice to a student's responses, but the text warns that the space between practice and learning is the weak spot.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In elementary math, Zearn is named as a program that works through adaptive practice. For older grades, Khan Academy is named as another program that works this way. In a middle school math class, the text gives an example of three days of adaptive practice and one short quiz on paper each week. The teacher compares the two, meaning the adaptive practice results and the paper quiz results. Across these grade bands, the teacher's part is to read what the software learned and use it to regroup students the next day.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence here as steadier than for most patterns. A review of 21 studies of AI in kindergarten through 12th grade math found a small positive effect, larger when the software acted as an intelligent tutor or adaptive system (Yi et al., 2024). A second review found that intelligent tutors helped K through 12 students in general, but that the advantage shrank when the comparison was other practice software rather than no software at all (Letourneau, 2025). For students with disabilities, a review of 29 studies found a medium sized effect (Zhang, 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The weak spot is the space between practice and learning. Practice scores can rise while real understanding stays flat, especially when students can game the software or lean on hints. That is why the idea in Chapter 7 keeps AI practice separate from regular checks done without the tool. In a middle school math class, this might mean three days of adaptive practice and one short quiz on paper each week, with the teacher comparing the two. The decisions that stay with a person are reading what the software learned, regrouping students, and comparing the practice results with the checks done without the tool.
